displayQuote: Last words are for fools who haven't said enough

meta.title: Who really said "Last words are for fools who haven't said enough"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Karl Marx as a deathbed retort to his housekeeper. No witness recorded it — Engels said Marx was left alone two minutes and never woke.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Last words are for fools who haven't said enough'?
meta.ogDescription: Marx's famous last words appear in no account of his death. Engels, at the graveside: he "had been left alone for scarcely two minutes."

answer.label: Not documented from Karl Marx
answer.authorDates: 5 May 1818 – 14 March 1883 · German philosopher and revolutionary socialist
answer.sourceLine: The line is printed everywhere as Marx’s answer to his housekeeper, who supposedly asked whether he had a last word for posterity — but it appears in no letter, memoir or newspaper report left by the people who were in the house. Friedrich Engels, who was there that afternoon and wrote to a comrade the next day, described a man who slipped away in silence: at the graveside on 17 March 1883 he said Marx “had been left alone for scarcely two minutes” ↗ and was found already gone.
answer.confidenceText: Widely credited to Marx, but unrecorded by anyone present and filed under “Disputed” by Wikiquote.

source.heading: What the record actually contains

docMeta.dd: None — no account by anyone present contains the line
Engels to Friedrich Adolph Sorge, 15 March 1883

source.excerpt: His housekeeper asked whether he had any last words for posterity. ‘Go on, get out! Last words are for fools who haven’t said enough.’
trail: Engels’s letter to Friedrich Adolph Sorge, London, 15 March 1883 ↗ is the fullest first-hand account of the death. It runs through the last months of illness, records Engels arriving at half past two the previous afternoon to find the house in tears, and reports the housekeeper’s only quoted words: that Marx was half asleep and he might come in. There is no retort in it.

Engels said the same thing publicly at the graveside at Highgate Cemetery on 17 March 1883 ↗: “On the 14th of March, at a quarter to three in the afternoon, the greatest living thinker ceased to think. He had been left alone for scarcely two minutes…” The speech was reprinted in Der Sozialdemokrat of 22 March 1883 ↗.

Wikiquote ↗ keeps the line in its Disputed list for Marx, with no source beyond “various attributions”. Quote Investigator, which has examined several Marx attributions, has never published on this one.

In print, the sentence belongs to the last-words anthology genre: Gyles Brandreth’s Famous Last Words and Tombstone Humour (New York: Sterling, 1989) ↗ is one such book, and a full-text search of scanned books ↗ finds it there and in more than a dozen similar collections, none of them citing a source.
source.excerptNote: That framing is the anthologies’ own; it is not a quotation from anyone who was in the house. Engels, who arrived that afternoon, wrote to Sorge the next day that Lenchen came downstairs to say Marx was half asleep, and that when they entered the room he was asleep “but never to wake again” — “In those two minutes he had passed away, peacefully and without pain.” ↗

sourceLink.text: Engels to F. A. Sorge, 15 March 1883 — Marxists Internet Archive

source.rightsNote: No work, letter, speech or newspaper report has ever been tied to this wording, so there is no first-publication date against which its copyright status could be judged — which is exactly why we do not label it public domain. Marx’s own writings and Engels’s 1883 accounts of his death are long out of copyright; this sentence is simply unsourced.

author.name: Karl Marx
author.kicker: The man it is pinned on
author.heading: Karl Marx
author.metaLine: 1818–1883 · German philosopher, political economist and revolutionary socialist
author.bio: Born in Trier in the Kingdom of Prussia on 5 May 1818, Marx spent his last decades as a stateless exile in London, writing Das Kapital and running a global correspondence from a house full of daughters, debts and unfinished manuscripts. He was, by every account, a spectacular talker and an even better insulter — which is precisely why a sharp deathbed one-liner sticks to him so easily. He died on 14 March 1883, in an armchair, with no one in the room.

cite.sourceCitation: No primary source located: the wording appears in no contemporary account of Marx’s death. It circulates through popular quotation anthologies — e.g. Gyles Brandreth, Famous Last Words and Tombstone Humour (New York: Sterling, 1989). Cf. Frederick Engels, letter to Friedrich Adolph Sorge, London, 15 March 1883, and Engels’s speech at the grave of Karl Marx, Highgate Cemetery, 17 March 1883 (printed in Der Sozialdemokrat, 22 March 1883).

copyAttribution: Karl Marx is popularly said to have snapped "Go on, get out! Last words are for fools who haven't said enough" at his housekeeper. No witness account records it. Friedrich Engels, at Marx's graveside on 17 March 1883, said Marx "had been left alone for scarcely two minutes" and was found already gone — no last words of his are recorded by anyone present. Checked by Quotle.info.

misattribution.heading: What's wrong with the story
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-shared “famous last words” in circulation, and nearly every version arrives with stage directions that no witness ever wrote down.

items.why: No letter, memoir, obituary or newspaper report from anyone present contains it. Wikiquote places the sentence in its Disputed section ↗, noting only “various attributions” — that is, popular repetition with no origin behind it.

items.scope: The housekeeper asking for a word for posterity
items.why: Engels’s letter of 15 March 1883 ↗ has her doing something quite different: she went upstairs, came back down, and said Marx was half asleep and Engels might come in. Wikipedia’s article on Demuth ↗ records no request for last words either.

Scanned-book snippets ↗ give “Go on, get out!”, “Get out of here and leave me alone” and no preamble at all, and one book adds “already” to the end. Wording that mutates freely from collection to collection is wording nobody is copying from a source.

misattribution.truthLine: The documented record is Engels’s, spoken over the grave at Highgate on 17 March 1883: Marx “had been left alone for scarcely two minutes” ↗ and was found already gone — no last words of his are recorded by anyone present.

context.heading: Why a man who said everything was given one more line
lead: Marx died in the afternoon of 14 March 1883, in the house in north London where he had spent his exile. Engels had made a habit of calling in the early afternoon; that day he arrived to find the household in tears. Helene “Lenchen” Demuth, the housekeeper who had run the Marx family for decades, went upstairs, came back down and said he was half asleep and Engels might go in. That is the last thing anyone reports her saying about him alive.

Three days later, standing over the grave at Highgate, Engels gave the sentence that has framed the scene ever since: “He had been left alone for scarcely two minutes, and when we came back we found him in his armchair, peacefully gone to sleep — but for ever.” ↗ A silence that complete leaves a very tempting gap. The quip fills it perfectly: it is what a reader wants the author of Das Kapital to have said, and it conveniently explains why nothing else was recorded.
context.detailsSummary: How the line behaves in print
detailsBody: A quote that was genuinely transmitted from a deathbed tends to stabilise: one witness, one wording, one place it is always cited from. This one does the opposite. A full-text search of scanned books ↗ shows it as “Go on, get out! Last words are for fools who haven’t said enough” in some collections, “Get out of here and leave me alone. Last words are for fools who haven’t said enough already” in another, and simply “Last words are for fools who haven’t said enough” in a third — with no anthology citing a source for any of them. One general quotation dictionary in that same search prints it in its Marx entry flagged only as attributed.

None of this proves Marx never grumbled something like it during his last illness; it proves that nobody wrote it down at the time, and that everything we have came later, from books whose business is a good closing line.
context.pull: He had been left alone for scarcely two minutes.

sourcesVerified.claim: Engels, writing to F. A. Sorge on 15 March 1883, describes arriving at 2.30 the previous afternoon, the housekeeper Lenchen coming downstairs to say Marx was half asleep, and that on entering 'he lay there asleep, but never to wake again... In those two minutes he had passed away, peacefully and without pain.' No last words are reported.

Engels's speech at the grave of Karl Marx, Highgate Cemetery, 17 March 1883, opens: 'On the 14th of March, at a quarter to three in the afternoon, the greatest living thinker ceased to think. He had been left alone for scarcely two minutes, and when we came back we found him in his armchair, peacefully gone to sleep -- but for ever.'
Der Sozialdemokrat of 22 March 1883 reported Marx's funeral of 17 March at Highgate and printed Engels's graveside speech in full.

Wikiquote's Karl Marx page lists 'Last words are for fools who haven't said enough.' in its Disputed section, sourced only as 'Various attributions'. (Confirmed by reading the page's raw wikitext, where the entry sits between the {{Disputed begin}} and {{Disputed end}} markers.)
The same Disputed-section entry, read directly from the page's raw wikitext.

A full-text search of scanned books returns the phrase in numerous last-words and quotation anthologies, in conflicting wordings — 'Go on, get out. Last words are for fools who haven't said enough' credited to Karl Marx, 'Leave me alone. Last words are for fools who haven't said enough already' as 'last words of Karl Marx', and an entry in a general quotation dictionary marked merely 'Attributed'.
Gyles Brandreth's 'Famous last words and tombstone humour' was published in 1989 by Sterling (New York), distributed in London by Cassell.

Wikipedia's article on Helene Demuth describes her as the Marx family's housekeeper and later Engels's household manager, and contains no mention of Marx's last words or of her asking him for a final message.
Karl Marx was born 5 May 1818 in Trier, Kingdom of Prussia, and died 14 March 1883; Wikipedia describes him as 'a German philosopher, social and political theorist, and revolutionary socialist'.
